claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by passive-film formation and stability.
The governing passive film has fewer defects.
The governing passive film contains more stable oxides.
Passive films with fewer defects and more stable oxides enhance corrosion resistance.
Passive-film formation and stability reduce total coupled wear-and-corrosion degradation.
Synergistic interaction between wear and corrosion leads to formation of a passive film with fewer defects and more stable oxides.
The proposed behavior applies in harsh environments containing high concentrations of corrosive species such as chloride.
The optimized passive-film condition will reduce total degradation by 30% relative to a baseline high-entropy alloy without optimized passive-film formation.
Both the wear and corrosion components of degradation will be reduced relative to the baseline.
The exact passive-film mechanism and its stability may vary with alloy composition.
The exact passive-film mechanism and its stability may vary with environmental conditions.
Varying load, speed, and corrosion medium in a controlled tribo-corrosion test can evaluate the effect of passive-film formation on total degradation.
Failure to obtain at least a 20% reduction in total degradation relative to the baseline falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says passive-film formation governs the wear-corrosion synergy, whereas the mechanism says the wear-corrosion synergy causes passive-film formation, creating reversed and circular causality.

The prediction specifies a 30% reduction, but the falsification rule accepts reductions from 20% to below 30%; such results would miss the stated prediction without falsifying it under the supplied rule.
